speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DISCOVERY OF OIL SATURATED SAND DEPOSIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that last year I was able to announce the issuance of new regulations for oil and gas exploration and development in the north. These regulations outlined a policy which it was anticipated would encourage continued effort not only on the mainland of the territories but also in the Arctic islands. Since that time a deep test well has been drilled on Melville island and over $1,100,000 have been spent on geological exploration in the islands.
It is my pleasure to announce today that a geological party of J. C. Sproule and Associates, working in the Marie bay area of northwest Melville island for permit holders including Canadian Oil Companies Limited, Bankeno Mines Limited and W. R. Sheeky, have discovered a large exposure of sand saturated with oil. Preliminary information indicates that the saturated oil sand is between 60 to 80 feet thick and is exposed at the surface for a distance of approximately 60 miles. While much work remains to be done before the full significance of this discovery can be determined, it does give tangible proof that oil is to be found in the Arctic islands.

Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked me a question in regard to the part played, as he said, by eight Canadian owned ships in trade between communist countries and Cuba, following which the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) used these words:
I should like to ask a supplementary question. Can control not be exercised over these ships or the companies owning them because of the fact that their profits are taxed in this country and the money goes into the federal treasury?
To this I replied that I had no information in that regard but would look into the matter. I now find that the owners of approximately 125 Canadian vessels were allowed, in 1949 and 1950, to register their ships in the United Kingdom under the transfer plan.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of hon. members on this side of the house approached me some weeks ago on this matter, as well as the various provincial governments in the maritimes. I had the question looked into. Incidentally another hon. member on the opposite side of the house, the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart), indicated his intention of asking this question today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like all those who have preceded me in this debate I wish to extend my congratulations to you and Mr. Deputy Speaker on your elevation to the high offices you hold. Though my words may be brief, and though your job is becoming more difficult, my thoughts for you are none the less sincere.
I extend the same compliments equally sincerely to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and before proceeding further I should like to pay tribute to the efforts put forth in this house by the deceased member for Wetaski-win, Mr. Speakman, on behalf of the veterans of Canada and in the field of agriculture, as well as all his other interests.
Before making any comments on the debate which has taken place so far I should also like to make some specific mention of the assistance that has been rendered to me by the ministerial benches. I particularly mention the Minister of Agriculture because I represent two counties in Ontario, the county of Grey and the county of Bruce for which, as well of course as for others, the minister has laid down a program the implementation of which, he assured me within the last few days, will be expedited.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, to whom I extend my gratitude for instituting, in conjunction with provincial authorities, a survey program for determining the feasibility of establishing a park in the Bruce peninsula. I also recognize the assistance given by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Robinson) and the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Noble). I hope this park will be
The Address-Mr. Winkler established in the vicinity of the terminating point of the Bruce trail, which will probably come to fruition in 1964 or 1965.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have some thoughts to put forward on things that have been said in this house. These subjects have been brought back to me in some cases by my constituents and in other cases by the newspapers which have some influence in the riding I have the priviiege to represent. They deal with the efforts of the official opposition to downgrade and vilify the Prime Minister of Canada, and hence the Canadian people. Unquestionably the Liberal party has downgraded the standards of political life. They have done this not only in the past but during the last few days in the course of this debate. For instance, there was the statement by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, which is to be found on page 216 of Hansard for October 4:
I might say, sir, that if anyone wants to see how the Prime Minister looked that day himself it is recorded on page 38 of Newsweek, the issue of July 2, and I commend it to the hon. gentlemen opposite.
That is a statement which is very definite in its implication, and there was a further statement by the same hon. member, to be found at page 218 of Hansard, when he made this remark in regard to the Minister of Justice:
He can get up and make a speech in this debate if he dares.
That was rather typical of the hon. gentleman from Bonavista-Twillingate. Earlier than that, as recorded at page 73 of Hansard for October 1, the leader of the official opposition said:
If the government tries to tell us that it has continued to play an increasingly effective role in international affairs, then I would ask it to present the evidence in support of that.
Then there was the statement made last evening by the leader of the official opposition replying to the invitation of the Minister of Finance, in which he said:
Presumably it was to apologize to the Prime Minister for what I have said about the attitude of the Prime Minister and his government on the common market-
There are other things I would like to comment on with regard to the interest shown by my constituency, by myself, and by other people who support the stand that we take.
First of all I regret that the Leader of the Opposition is not present, because I wish to remind him that on many occasions and in many circumstances I supported him because of his type of personality and the type of man he was, in the past, but not the type he has now become. Some time before the end of the

The Address-Mr. Winkler last parliament he made a speech in my home town of Hanover in which he said:
Our influence as a country abroad has diminished.
This will be found in the Owen Sound Sun-Times of that date. There are many other such quotations that I could use. I could refer to the one used by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, from a speech made by the former minister of public works when he stated Canada was on the verge of bankruptcy. I could also refer to another statement made by the same man at Sherbrooke, Quebec, when he said that Canada's prestige had been lowered and it had even lost the confidence of its own people at home. If these were not deliberate efforts to downgrade our country and our political life, then I am afraid I must be wasting my time here. I say that because it is the type of representation in this house and the support and assistance I have received, in my own experience, from the ministers of the crown that permit me to stay here in my own good conscience to serve the people of my constituency, and not the sort of thing that has been coming from the other side, particularly from the senior members.
Let us go back a step further, Mr. Speaker. This all did not happen in very recent times. For instance, we recall the many, many speeches made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the great effort he made to play up the circumstances that existed when we were having a difficult time finding employment for all the workers of this country.
I refer hon. members to a newspaper article published in the Galt Evening Reporter by one of the local members of the press gallery. He said:
The Hon. Paul "Mother Goose" Martin is spreading his fairy tales with a heavier hand than ever. But it is as a wicked fairy that he continues his three year old campaign of smearing Canada as a country of misery, depression and unemployment.
This was about the hon. member for Essex East, and you will note, Mr. Speaker, that he has been rather quiet of late; just a little bit quiet.

speechtext: You are going to arouse me if you continue.

speechtext:
We know why. Is he now unhappy because a lot of Canadians are working, more than ever before in the history of our country? This reporter goes on to say, of the hon. member for Essex East:
Would not his pulse quicken with glee, if he could rise in the house and talk about one million Canadians out of work?
But it is a regrettable effort on the part of the hon. member for Essex East. That is


not all. I could go on all day, but I have chosen these examples because I am endeavouring to prove that the members of that party did what they could to the best of their ability to downgrade this country and vilify its leaders, particularly the Prime Minister. This quotation comes from the Owen Sound Sun-Times, the only daily printed in the vicinity of my constituency. It is the issue of February 10, 1962, after the hon. member for Essex East made a terrific attack on the government's policy of endeavouring to get people back to work. The commentary was this:
And, as so often is the case of such critics, he took the risk of actually harming the nation's economy to attain his end.
I wonder what that end is. I do not think it is very difficult for hon. members of this house to see, although it may not be the same in all quarters of the country. It might be wise at this time to warn the leader of the official opposition that he has other problems to deal with. Perhaps the hon. member for Essex East is sitting in his quietude and waiting for a campaign to start on that side of the house; or perhaps it would be the former minister of public works, in view of that speech in Lunenburg and Sherbrooke, Quebec, who is waiting; or would the elections in Quebec have any connotation regarding what we might expect as the leadership of the Liberal party in the near future? I do not know; but it all looks very, very significant to me.
Then let us consider what the country had to read about statements that were made regarding the Prime Minister's efforts overseas in relationship to Britain's entry into the common market. I will read from the Ottawa Journal. I admit that here we can perhaps expect a little sympathy for our stand and our views. Here two questions appear in regard to statements made about Canada in the commentaries of newspapers of Great Britain. This article specifically mentions the Observer, the Sunday Telegraph, and so on. The two questions posed are these:
(1) Who inspired these offscourings in the London Observer, and (2) does Mr. Lester Pearson, who from Ottawa kept stabbing Mr. Diefenbaker in the back every day he was in London, go along with them?
These were very derisive statements. I am sure most hon. members have read them. I wonder if that is true. Certainly his activity all through the period when the Prime Minister was out of the country will require some sensible answer, if it is possible, to those two questions. Or I wonder, does the Leader of the Opposition not understand that without putting forth a strong view and a strong stand at that time, Britain's own position

35S
would be weakened upon going into the common market. It would have been weakened today. Not only our Prime Minister, who may have taken the lead and I hope he did-but every prime minister of the commonwealth understands that when the time comes for Britain to enter the common market, not only should there be a strong political union, but our rights and privileges should not be lost. We wish to feel as important a part of the commonwealth in the future as we have in the past. Our contribution, Mr. Speaker, as you know, has been a very substantial one.
How far will the Liberals go to smear a leader, a policy or a country? I hold in my hands-hon. members may possibly have seen it-a pamphlet without any heading, not being authorized by anyone, which is headed on the back, "Can the deceivers govern?" On the front page there are two pictures of the Prime Minister, in one of which he is very well dressed and in the other he is supposedly in rags. One picture is dated June 18, 1962 and the other June 25. This may be all in the course of putting their propaganda to the country, but let me tell you, Mr. Speaker and hon. members of this house, that this was a piece of literature that came to me from the Liberal booth at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto. How did it come to me? It came to me through a gentleman who is concerned with the export of Canadian goods out of this country, who does quite a substantial amount of business with the Chinese nationalists.
This was handed to a Mr. Wu, who is the Chinese trade commissioner from Taipei. What can we expect outside this country if they try to dish this out at one of the places where we have international figures coming in to buy our products? Can we expect any increase in trade? It is a wonder to me that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is meeting with any success whatsoever in his programs, and it is a wonder that such booths are set up at places where these international buyers can come and buy our products. It is a wonder to me, also, that these people do not put up loudspeakers and tell them not to buy. That is what they are trying to do, and they are not making too bad a job of it.

I also want to thank and congratulate the mover (Mr. Chaplin) and the seconder (Mr. Vincent) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Mr. Speaker, as it is the first time I have the privilege of sitting in this imposing assembly, I should also like to commend all members of the staff, in the external as well as the internal services, for their courtesy and for the prompt and kindly way in which they fulfil their respective tasks and duties.
The atmosphere, the spaciousness and size of this house, as well as its comfortable set-up should, to my mind, incite hon. members who sit here to establish in Canada an economic system inspired by the comforts which surround us in this august chamber.
Mr. Speaker, the night of June 18 last we, and more particularly the French Canadians in the province of Quebec, gave a sigh of relief. Considering that, in our province, which had been called Liberal for almost a hundred years, Liberal governments had always been elected, except in 1957, and more particularly in my riding, where the people had voted Liberal for 68 consecutive years, we cannot but give a big sigh of relief.
My predecessor was a member of parliament for 17 years. Yet, yesterday, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) tendered him his congratulations, whereas he knew very well that, like the others he named yesterday, my predecessor had lost out and been rejected by the people and the voters of his county in the June 18 election. For 17 years, my riding had been Liberal, and, for 68 years, the voters in the province of Quebec had voted in favour of the Liberal party.
[Mr. Laing.)
Now, we begin to breathe again, to feel freer. We begin to feel the effects of a new economic system which will, perhaps, not be at the mercy of the old parties that have led the province of Quebec, and the whole of Canada, into the economic stagnation we are having today.
We obtained a clear vote on June 18 last, and we shall win a greater victory in the future. Some people looked upon the Social Credit vote in the province of Quebec on June 18 as a tidal wave, but I think that at the next general election, the tide will sweep away all the political rats, more particularly in our province.
At the first public meeting I held in my riding after the election of last June 18, I did not hold a press conference as was suggested yesterday in this house. It was only an organization meeting where I expressed the hope that the house proceedings would be televised during at least one hour every day. If the people could have witnessed the behaviour of some members of this house during the past week, they would have found out the truth about, first of all, their turpitude, their trivialities and their empty words and they would also have seen how those members beat around the bush for an hour's time or four hours on end, as the leader of the Liberal opposition did, to achieve absolutely nothing. Our constituents, who, in addition to being taxpayers, are also those who provide the funds to finance the C.B.C., should be the first to know what goes on in this august assembly. I feel it would not be too much to ask to have the parliament debates televised an hour each day, so that the people could be informed directly, instead of being given a falsified account, of what goes on in this house.
Mr. Speaker, we are not here to play into the hands of the old parties or to lend ourselves to the Liberal practice of seeking a means to overthrow the government overnight. Did not the Liberals themselves deplore the fact, and rightly so, that France experienced nothing but temporary governments which changed from one day to the next? We do not wish to see Canada in a similar situation. And that is why we of the Social Credit party shall not play into the hands of the Liberals, who are seeking to overthrow the government tomorrow or the day after or next week, to end up in that same situation which we do not want.

The Address-Mr. Rondeau
We do not wish to keep the Conservatives in power just for the fun of it, but for one purpose only, and that is to obtain better legislation for Canada and for all Canadians.
To us, the important thing is not to change the seats of the pants on the benches in parliament but it is rather to amend the legislation which in the near future will govern the destiny of our people. We want legislation and we do not intend to be satisfied with empty promises, or beautiful phrases or billing and cooing on the part of the Conservatives, to get nowhere. We are ready to co-operate. We are willing to assist. We are ready to give them an opportunity either to legislate for the common good of the Canadian people or to weave the rope they will be hanged with at the next federal election.
We want better laws from the government. Among other things, we want family allowances proportionate to the cost of living index. When family allowances were initiated in 1945, milk sold at 8 to 10 cents a quart, but the cost of living has increased threefold since then, while family allowances have been increased by a single dollar. For that reason, on behalf of my constituents and of Canadians throughout the country, I ask that family allowances be proportionate to the present cost of living index.
I also request an adjustment in old age pensions. Our older people must live just as our younger people. The rate of old age pension was not adjusted since the adoption of the act. I, therefore, request that it be proportionate to the cost of living index.
I request also for the small wage earner, the worker, the farmer, all those who build the real wealth of Canada and of our province, an exemption of taxes as being heads of families. Such an exemption should be at least $5,000 for the head of a family and $3,000 for a single person. Statistics show that it costs at least $86 a week to live, to give the bare necessities to a family of five. If such is the case it is only logical and normal for us in this house to request a total exemption of tax for all salaried people earning less than $100 a week.
We also want, Mr. Speaker, more encouragement for private enterprise.
In 1962, everybody is against private enterprise. Public bodies, aldermen, municipal councils, provincial governments and even the federal government are grabbing private enterprise by the throat. We are trying to crush it by imposing heavy taxes upon it,
and in one province in particular there is even some talk of nationalization. Yet, it is thanks to private enterprise if we have prosperity in Canada right now.
It is neither the Liberals, during their 22 years in office, nor the Conservatives, in the last five years, who have made Canada what it is today.
If Canada is rich and prosperous in 1962, if she has abundant natural resources, if her production is high, that is not due to any government but to private enterprise, because private enterprise was the one to understand the situation in our country.
We rise to the defence of private enterprise. If we do not save it, we will soon live to regret it. In fact, a country which is 1,800 miles away from here but which is quite close to the U.S.A., Cuba, was in the same situation not so long ago. Today, everybody deplores the way things turned out there.
There were millionaires in Cuba before the communists took over; there was private enterprise and also the proletariat, workers and farmers. Came the day when those people had enough of being exploited and crushed by taxes. Revolution started to brew and Castro entered the scene. Under the guise of planning, of state socialism, he removed private enterprise and established a totalitarian government which handed the country over to the communists. We Social Crediters knew already that the Liberals were socialist and that the socialists were Liberals. We fully understand their stand in this house, we know why they want economic planning and nationalization of our business concerns.
We of the Social Credit do not advocate the nationalization of private enterprise.
I am an industrialist, and my problem is not to produce but to sell the goods; my problem is to face farmers in need, to face farmers who need my products, but who must live in debt for five or 10 years in order to purchase today what I can produce and manufacture today.
Our economic system, as it stands today, does not allow our farmers, our workers to live today, in this country of ours, with the money they earn today and to buy what is produced today. They have to go into hock for many years to come.
That is the baseness of the present system. We have been elected to fight against this system, and that is the reason I want to be

The Address-Mr. Rondeau the prime defender of the people of my constituency who elected me. I have not been elected to be a supporter of the Liberal and Conservative policies, but for the sole purpose of seeking improved legislation for the farmer, the worker, the small businessman and the individual who is still self-employed.
Everybody is crying for the opening of new markets abroad and no one is looking at the markets we have here in our communities, our provinces and across Canada.
Once upon a time, two gentlemen were admiring a beautiful mountain. One said to the other "Do you see that mountain in front of you?" And the other replied "Indeed I do" and the first gentleman went on: "Can you see the fly on the mountain?" The other replied "No, I cannot see it on the mountain because it is on the tip of your nose."
Well, Mr. Speaker, when we see Conservative or Liberal politicians wracking their brains in order to find ways and means to sell Canadian goods throughout the world, while there are so many people who need them here at home, we are inclined to tell them: Instead of going outside Canada, why not try to sell from door to door in our cities or in our municipalities. Visit our farmers, our workers, our small contractors, see what the needs are in the province of Quebec, and then you will realize that we do not need to send commissioners in other countries in order to sell our products, we can sell a lot of them right here, in our own country.
Let us ask ourselves why it is that so many firms, so many plants, so many businesses have to close their doors at the present time or have to lay off some of their employees because of a lack of orders.
Let us ask ourselves why, in my own constituency, for instance, over 600 employees from three different plants were laid off.
Let us ask ourselves why, in the constituency of St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, workers were laid off by the hundreds not later than last week, although it is said that we have enough buying power in Canada.
If we do not lack buying power in this country, why do we try to sell our products to the tourists? Why woo the American tourists? Why woo the foreign tourists? In order to extort dollars from them in exchange for our products.
Production in Canada is well known for its quality and its variety. Those who will set up a system-and we want to do it-that will

enable Canadians to live in a wealthy country, where production is not lacking, those will not remain in power during 22 years, instead power will be theirs for the rest of their lives.
At the present time, people say jokingly that we want to form a coalition with the Conservatives. Such is not the case.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) is in a dilemma. His own supporters, after suffering two defeats, would like a new leader. And because his party was defeated twice, that gentleman would like to have an election as soon as possible, in order to prevent the Liberals from choosing a new leader.
Last night, when the non-confidence motion proposed by the official opposition was put to a vote, several Liberal members had not been consulted. They were asked to vote although they had not been consulted before. And several have told us of their surprise.
We do not want to get caught at the game of "old gimmicks" nor do we want to get involved in the old game of petty politics. Our mandate is clear and simple, and we want to serve the voters of our ridings and those of the province of Quebec especially.
Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec elected the Liberal party for 22 years, in Ottawa, and I must say today in this house that it is the province which has been the most badly treated.
The Liberal party is shocked and offended in considering that its favoured province, the province on which it thought it had forever a grip, has forsaken it.
Today they realize that Social Credit, on June 18 last, achieved a break through which we shall continue to enlarge, not only in this house, but also during the next election, which may be not far off. We are going to wipe off the political map of the province of Quebec, not only the Liberal party but the old parties who have not been able to give Canadians prosperity in our province, as in other provinces, whereas Canada has all it needs to yield that prosperity.
The small retailer, the industrialist and private enterprise want a prosperous Canada.
What we want, is not a planning government, not a government with socialist leanings, not a government which is perpetually searching our pockets. What we want is a government with sound business principles. We do not want the government to be mixed

up in our business, but we want sound business principles in the government.
If, in the past, legislation had been based on sound business principles, we would not now have to deplore the fact that Canada has a terrible debt which is increasing every day.
Canada has known and still knows today, a period of recession. We are still going through times where private enterprise is exhausted and gives all its benefits away in taxes. The proof, Mr. Speaker, is that today our savings capital is swallowed up by public works.
People have lost confidence in the administration of Canada, but not in private enterprise. Why is that? Because, today, our savings capital goes to finance sidewalks, water mains, bridges, sewers and public works.
If people had confidence in private enterprise, in this country, they would not be interested in financing public works.
That is why we ask, as did the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), that a municipal development bank be established to give municipalities in our province, and throughout Canada, a source of credit which would help carry out their public works. We should not finance public works with our savings. The money we have saved should be used to finance private production, and public capital made available to our governments should be used to finance public works.
Mr. Speaker, people complain at this time- and justly so-that our national economy, and also our provincial economy, are slipping into the hands of other countries and of international finance. We need hardly be surprised at that fact, when our own government does not even make available to our private industries the capital they need to finance their projects. We must draw from our savings capital to finance 50- to 100-year projects.
It is about time, Mr. Speaker, to stop laughing at Social Credit proposals. It is very easy to laugh at a certain thing, one has only to twitch one's face and that's it, but it takes much less intelligence to laugh at something than to understand it.
Before June 18, many were those who were laughing at Social Credit proposals, as well as at the Social Credit philosophy. Many were those who were laughing at all that, but on the evening of June 18, they got the lesson of their lives.
The Address-Mr. Fulton
We shall keep on explaining to the people what is Social Credit; we shall keep on explaining to the people that we have not been elected here by means of election funds which would tie us to national or international financiers who would like farmers to be still exploited by companies which have contributed to both parties' funds.
My election cost only a few thousand dollars, about ten times less than the campaign of the one who was defeated after sitting here for 17 years, wearing out the seat of his pants to such an extent that one day he was so mixed up-and those who were here at the time will remember the incident- in his absent-mindedness he voted against his own party. By the way, he asked the Speaker to correct his mistake, and to record his vote as his party wished it.
Having been defeated on June 18 last, he is now trying to find himself another place in provincial politics. Well, I wish him the same fate he has known on June 18, in order that all these jokers of our province and of our country disappear before long from the political map of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, those few minutes were put at my disposal to serve and represent the electors of my constituency who gave me a wonderful majority on June 18. I congratulate them and I shall try in this house to serve them with honour and to be always at their disposal.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your good attention.

speechtext:
May I take this opportunity of associating myself publicly, as I have already done privately, with those who have extended to you, Mr. Speaker, their congratulations and compliments upon the occasion of your elevation to this high office? May I also associate myself with the things which have been said in complimenting the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne? With respect to yourself, Mr. Speaker, it is naturally a matter of particular pleasure to me, coming as I do from your neighbouring province in the west, to see you occupying the chair in this house, not only a fellow western Canadian but one who in his person combines also the two major racial divisions of this country.

The Address-Mr. Fulton
To the mover and the seconder of the address in reply I wish merely to say this, in addition to what I have already said. I desire them to know that I experienced profound admiration for the way in which they discharged their duties here. That admiration was perhaps tinged with a little bit of envy because I recall that on the occasion of my maiden speech I was far from acquitting myself with the distinction with which they acquitted themselves in a much more onerous position, having undertaken as they had the much more onerous task of moving the address in reply to His Excellency. It is an onerous task not only because of the fact that it is a difficult and nerve wracking burden on a new member but because, as I am sure they would agree, Mr. Speaker, and as they themselves indeed said, it fell to them to move the address in reply to one of the most important and far reaching throne speeches that have been laid before this house.
As we are now nearing the end of a time allotted for the debate on the address, it is perhaps not inappropriate to spend a few moments in review, as it were, of what has taken place during this debate. One of the things, of course, that marks the debate on this occasion, is the fact that we have seen moved in the house a variety of amendments, all of which have raised the question of whether this government should continue to have the responsibility of governing. On those amendments, I am glad to remind you, Mr. Speaker, the government has been sustained by a majority of the members of this house. Of course, this result but confirms the verdict which the people of Canada recorded on June 18. It is not inappropriate to recall that on that day, under our system, the Canadian people entrusted the continued responsibility of government to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the present government and thus far this house has sustained that verdict.
One can therefore understand the obvious frustration of the Liberal party, a frustration arising not only from their experience to date in this house but out of the fact that they have made three attempts in the last five years in carrying their case to the people to take over the responsibility of office and that in all those attempts they have failed. In the last attempt we saw the most desperate scramble for power in Canada's history. In the course of that attempt, culminating on June 18, we saw the Liberal party stop at nothing in their efforts to translate into reality their highly imaginative lust for power. After all, I suppose one could almost sympathize


with them in their frustration. Three times they have tried and on the night of June 18, Mr Speaker, you will recall what happened. I am sure you watched with me, as I am sure did many other hon. members, the Leader of the Opposition when he appeared on television so confident that he was going to be able to drink the wine of victory. How frustrating it must have been to have that cup so rudely dashed from his lips at the last moment before he had really tasted a drop. Hence he is left now only to drain the dregs of the cup of bitterness. We recall these things.
As I say, one can sympathize to an extent with the members of the Liberal party in their frustration. However, as they seem to have forgotten it, it is perhaps as well to remind them that while they lust for power, there is one essential requirement which they have not yet met, namely that they win the largest number of seats in this house, if they are to have that responsibility. This fact they continue to overlook. However, until that event takes place or that remote possibility occurs, with the support of this house the responsibility of government rests upon this party and this government under the present Prime Minister of Canada. We accept that responsibility.
It is my view that the Canadian people, as they look towards their parliament now, expect the government upon which they imposed that responsibility on June 18, to respect it and to discharge it. The Canadian people expect this government to offer them a program designed to meet the problems with which this country is confronted. In accordance with that expectation and in accordance with our responsibility we have introduced that program into this house by way of the speech from the throne. It is a conscientious and, in my submission, a constructive program designed to meet today's problems and to lay a further foundation for the coming long range problems and requirements of tomorrow. That program represents no compromise or concession. It represents nothing by way of a deal or a special arrangement with any party or group. It is the government's own program which we have worked out to deal with the problems for the solution of which we are responsible. Thus far that program has been accepted by a majority in this house, although opposition parties in the house on various occasions have attempted to defeat that program.
In the time at my disposal this evening I propose to elaborate somewhat on the constructive actions and detailed programs which we lay before the house and country. First, however, in order that it may better be seen in perspective, it may be helpful if I deal for

a moment or two with the background or the backdrop against which that program is presented. The salient feature of that backdrop is, of course, the Liberal tactics which were started prior to the election campaign, reached their climax as it progressed, and then continued in this house as well as outside of it since that time. I refer to the scream and scare tactics which characterize the current approach of the Liberal party to Canadian problems. A little earlier I said that during the election campaign they stopped at nothing in their desire to achieve power. We saw them indulging in a tactic of attempting to create panic and confusion in the business and financial community. I shall give some examples of each of these criticisms. For this one, I think particularly of the example of a prominent Liberal businessman who, speaking in Truro, Nova Scotia, in early June said that Canada was teetering on the verge of bankruptcy.

We heard them uttering cries about the financial crisis while they themselves proposed measures that would add at least a billion dollars to the Canadian tax bill or the Canadian deficit. The Leader of the Opposition talks about irresponsibilitiy. He says now, as he said then, that he knew there was a financial crisis. Yet he deliberately advocated measures which, if he knew there was a financial crisis, he must also have known would add immeasurably to that crisis.
That is their tactic, Mr. Speaker, charges of misrepresentation and misleading while they themselves indulge in the most coldblooded misrepresentation and distortion of policy that has ever been seen in the record of political campaigns in this country.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have effectively given the lie to these charges in so far as they are applied to the government, but let us look for a moment at the tactics followed by the Liberal party during that campaign. Virtually every policy, in many cases policies which they themselves had advocated or knew to be right, for political purposes they distorted, misrepresented and criticized as being wrong and leading the country to the brink of disaster.
I think of some prominent examples. There is the policy of devaluation. Did you ever see such a spectacle as these prominent advocates of a policy of devaluation, a policy they knew
The Address-Mr. Fulton to be to the advantage of Canada and which they had advocated before they became Liberal candidates, turning around and adopting an attitude and associating themselves with and participating actively in a campaign which would have had the Canadian people believe that the policy of devaluation was the worst policy that the country could follow? I think particularly of such members as the member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) and the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Nicholson) who were prominent in urging upon the government that we should follow a policy of devaluation; and when we did, and in the light of the fact that it was having the results it was calculated to have in that industries in Canada were benefiting, we then saw these members go about distorting and misrepresenting not only their own position but the effects and the nature of the policy. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) placed before the house a list of commodities today which are exported from British Columbia and Canada, but he forbore to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that every industry producing these commodities has been immeasurably helped in British Columbia by the devaluation policy of the government.
What did the Liberal party say about the cost of living, coupling this with devaluation? They attempted to strike fear into the hearts of the Canadian people on the grounds that devaluation would lead to astronomical rises in the cost of living. The Leader of the Opposition, speaking in Halifax on June 8, a popular day for misstatements on the part of the Liberal party, was it not, Mr. Speaker, said words to the effect that the Canadian cost of living can rise to a point where it would be very dangerous indeed. What happened to the cost of living, Mr. Speaker? The fact of the matter is that the cost of living has remained satisfactorily stable in the months since. The campaign began in April, and yet between the months of August and September the cost of living experienced an appreciable drop. Again, the hon. member for Vancouver South, having reinherited the tactic of the selective use of statistics which is, after all, characteristic of members of the Liberal party, proceeded to quote some statistics from the dominion bureau of statistics in his speech today; but he conveniently overlooked the fact that the cost of living as a whole has dropped and that the major reason for that drop is a decline in the cost of food index. This is the very index that the Liberal party said repeatedly during the campaign would be sent up out of sight as a result of the policy of devaluation.
Nobody can be unconcerned if there is an increase in the cost of living, and there has

The Address-Mr. Fulton been an increase over all between April and September. But the fact of the matter is that by comparison with previous years there has not been as great a rise between April and September of 1962 as was the custom in those earlier years. Therefore one can see the extent to which this tactic was used by the Liberal party to mislead the Canadian people.
Finally, we see the tactic, unprecedented in the history of Canada, Mr. Speaker, indeed, I should think unprecedented in the history of the western world, of a direct and deliberate attack on the nation's currency, an onslaught on the integrity of the Canadian dollar, an attack on confidence itself.

Attacks on policy, of course, may oe expected and should be expected, particularly during an election campaign; but as for attacks on confidence in the currency, never before have I seen and never again will I see, I hope, a tactic such as that, destructive of confidence in the very integrity of our currency. Never again, I hope, will we see such a tactic such as that policy because confidence in the dollar outlives governments and parliament if it is maintained; and if it is destroyed it is more important and is a greater loss than the passage of any government or the demise of any particular parliament. This is what my hon. friends lost sight of, driven to the lengths of irresponsibility that they were in their lust for power.
I know that someone has said or maybe suggested: why do you rehash the election campaign? This is not just a rehash of the election campaign because unfortunately these tactics are still continuing. The fact of the matter is that apparently it is still the view and objective of the Liberal party that on the self-imposed ruins of the nation's currency, if they had their way, on the backs of Canadian workers and consumers whose devastation they would have encompassed, they would build a political future for themselves.
It is a continuing policy. We still see them in their frustration continuing their attempts to destroy confidence on the part of the Canadian people in their institutions, trying to capitalize on the fact that the country has a minority government by seeking to intimidate and frighten investors, businessmen and people generally with regard to the course of events. As authority for this statement I cite words used by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) speaking in the Stormont byelection campaign, as reported in the Montreal Star of July 13. He said:
Their minority will not stand. We can destroy it at a moment's notice ... at the opportune time.


Could any words be more calculated to inspire and instil lack of confidence in those who are looking, as they are entitled to look and expect, for stability in the affairs of our government? "Destroy it at a moment's notice, at the opportune time", even though the Canadian people had entrusted them with the responsibility of government, before they had any chance to submit their program to the house.

Under our system, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people entrusted us with the responsibility of government and until the hon. member for Essex East gets that through his head I fear he will be doomed to sit in frustration on the other side of the house.
With this approach, Mr. Speaker, I should like to contrast the program which we have offered this house and the country. As I have said, we accept the responsibility for government. We are fully conscious of the fact that we are a minority government but that fact does not relieve us of the responsibility of governing. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you, and it our view, that it but heightens the responsibility that we must show. So we have come before the house with a program of working, building and planning. That is the aim of the program embodied in the speech from the throne.
I should like to give the house some illustrations of it by referring to the work and planning of my own department, but I also think I can illustrate it effectively by contrasting it in the course of my remaining remarks with that ragtag and bobtail collection of left-over bits and pieces that the Leader of the Opposition tried to characterize as a program toward the end of the speech which he delivered on Tuesday of last week.
First, as to planning, Mr. Speaker, let me point out to the house that in spite of the fact we have had to implement emergency measures in my department, and there are some restrictions on physical construction, we have not in any way interfered with the planning vote of that department. Therefore, the vote of $1.5 million under which the planning of major and minor projects is carried on is untouched. Those plans are going forward so that at the earliest moment, when other factors permit, the plans can be implemented for the people of Canada.
Next, I should like to say a word with regard to physical activity, working and building. The Leader of the Opposition calls for a massive increase in construction. Let me refer to the July figures. Building permits issued for construction amounted to over $273 million for the month of July alone, up 20.2

per cent from a year earlier. The Leader of the Opposition says that half a billion dollars of construction means the equivalent of a year's work for 100,000 men, and their employment in turn would mean stimulation for a great deal of other business. This reference is found at page 70 of Hansard.
May I point out that permits issued in July for construction amounted to over a quarter of a billion dollars. If we have another month like July, we will have the half a billion dollars in construction ready to get under way and the 100,000 men to whom the Leader of the Opposition referred will be going back to work under Conservative policy.
May I refer the house to an item which appeared in the Gazette of October 9, which reads as follows:
Construction contract awards during the first nine months total $2,525 million-5.6 per cent higher than for the same period last year, according to the MacLean Building Guide. The increase derives from more housing and business construction con-ceentrated in the Quebec and Ontario areas.
These are some of the positive achievements and programs. The Leader of the Opposition speaks of the Liberals' national plan for municipal development. He speaks in the same breath of the colossal failure of our proposal and then goes on, in the same breath, to advocate more of the same. Let me give you some of the particulars of what has been done in this field in the years from 1957 up to August, 1962. There have been
724,000	new dwellings started in Canada, 45 per cent of which are financed under the National Housing Act, and $1.5 billion have been advanced in direct Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans during that period. There have been 20,000 units of rental accommodation provided for low income families, in an aggregate amount of $157 million.
The next item concerns some 5,000 public housing units which have been approved under the federal-provincial partnership arrangement since we took office; some 3,300 land assembly lots have been approved; approximately $675,000 have been contributed to urban renewal studies. Forty four such studies have been undertaken in the five years since the Conservative government was first elected, whereas there were six under the Liberals.
The Leader of the Opposition speaks of urban redevelopment. If I may paraphrase his own words used in another context, he thinks this program is as new as his own knowledge of it. The total contribution approved for urban redevelopment purposes under this government has been close to $20
The Address-Mr. Fulton million. Then, again, he speaks of sewage disposal. He criticizes, Mr. Speaker, but carefully omits to point out that it was this government that amended the National Housing Act, in December, 1960, to provide for sewage disposal projects and to assist municipalities. Since that time, 264 loans totalling over $68 million have been made and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has now some 271 preliminary applications on hand with a loan potential of another $67 million. This is the first time in the history of this country that a direct attack has been made on the joint problems of pollution and water conservation, the first time in the history of this country any constructive approach has been made to the problem of helping the municipalities whose need in this field was so desperate.
I could go on. The greatest tribute, I may say, should be paid to my predecessor, the Hon. David Walker, for the vision he had and the broad concept that he had in bringing this legislation into effect. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but in fact we have spent the last five years in working, building and planning in areas ignored by the Grits. I say without hesitation that if, in fact, there is a national concept of municipal development, it rests with this government and this party. The plans and the programs that I have outlined indicate the truth of that statement.
Coupled with that, I say that further imaginative, practical plans are to come. As an example of what I have in mind, I may say that I am asking Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to study three important and closely related matters. The first of these is in the broad field of providing housing for the physically handicapped; second, the study of a proposal to build university residences for married couples; third, the general question of the further application of the sewage disposal plan.
I think I have said enough. I hope I have said enough, Mr. Speaker, to show, particularly by way of contrast as against the scare and scream tactics of the Liberals, that we have for this country a constructive program of planning, building and working. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and his colleagues would have the business of the country grind to a halt, they would have Canadian and foreign investors run from the country, they would have this parliament become little less than a forum for their scream and scare tactics, they would have everybody stop and wait while they make their play for power. We cannot allow the government, parliament and people of Canada to be intimidated by threats such as the one used by the hon. member for Laurier, that they can

The Address-Mr. Mackasey destroy us at a moment's notice at an opportune time. No, Mr. Speaker, it is the electors of Canada who will determine when any opportune time comes, on the basis of which any government will be defeated.
I believe it is our duty, Mr. Speaker, and we accept the duty and responsibility of placing our program before this house, bringing in the detailed legislation by which this program will be implemented. On that basis, I invite the support of this house without compromise or concession. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we can leave to the hon. member for Laurier and other members of the Liberal party such ideas as they believe will destroy us, and that they will destroy this program at a moment's notice at the opportune time. What an arrogant statement. I suggest to hon. members of the Liberal party, in spite of their bravado, that they well know if, for opportunism such as they wish, they were able-they will not be able-to succeed in frustrating this constructive program and deprive this parliament of an opportunity of seeing this program implemented, it would be the most inopportune thing that could happen to them as well as being disastrous for Canada.
On the basis of the program, Mr. Speaker, I say to you that the Conservative government, the Conservative party, is prepared to go ahead and accept that responsibility of giving constructive government which the people have imposed upon us, satisfied when the proper moment comes to face the people on the basis of that program and that record. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I be
allowed, Mr. Speaker, like many others, to offer you my congratulations for your appointment to the high office you now occupy. My short experience in the house has already convinced me that the welfare of our country depends, to a large extent, on the integrity and impartiality with which you fulfil your functions.
May I be allowed also to congratulate the mover (Mr. Chaplin) and the seconder (Mr. Vincent) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The quality of those first two speeches has set a standard that all members will no doubt wish to emulate.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, as I stand here to speak for the first time in the House of Commons I do so with mixed emotions. I am very proud of being part of this house and representing the English speaking population of the province of Quebec. It is traditional, and perhaps in the spirit of democracy, that they have picked a backbencher to represent them here today, but at the same time I realize very humbly that I speak in the presence of so many
[Mr. Fulton.)
distinguished parliamentarians, men I have admired and respected, men who are sitting on both sides of the house.
I have just listened with great interest to the Minister of Public Works. I listened with concern as he expressed his disapproval of our attack on the monetary system of Canada during the election, but I say in all sincerity that it was not the printing of funny money or our remarks on the monetary system which caused a run on the Canadian dollar. It was the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture when he blithely admitted that it did not matter whether the dollar stood at 95 cents or 90 cents, and that they could decide by a flip of a coin that it should be 92 J. One cannot have respect for a government when one hears such talk from a minister of the crown.
Yesterday I listened with great respect to the Minister of Justice when he sprang to the defence of the deputy attorney general of Canada. With great indignation he stood up for this gentleman who, allegedly, was attacked by a member of the New Democratic party. What a contrast was his defence of the deputy attorney general to his behaviour in the Coyne affair.
Mr. Speaker, I am conscious of the fact that there is a new sense of awareness in the country. Never before in the peacetime history of Canada have so many people looked to parliament for leadership. Never before have so many people looked so desperately for some guidance and reassurance, for a plan to be formulated to show that leadership is available, leadership that will put the country back on the road to recovery. Like a man who has had his first heart attack this country realizes all is not sound with its economy. Its people are bewildered at the fact that there is no indication of a plan for the recovery of the economy, and they are anxious because the government does not take them into its confidence and confront them with the problems impeding our progress.
I am convinced that had the government introduced its austerity program a year sooner the people of Canada would look more favourably on the government than they do today. The people are ready, in a manner reminiscent of their wartime effort, to work, to increase production, to put their shoulders to the wheel if only the direction and leadership were available. Unfortunately the government is not taking advantage of this desire to face the facts. Rather, it is once again assuring the country that all is well, that unemployment is vanishing at a rapid rate and that in the very near future everyone will be back to work. For the sake of the unemployed I hope so.

The people remember the days when the prestige of Canada was at an all time high, when Canada's voice was a powerful one in the United Nations. They recall the time when the economy of Canada was strong and vigorous. Those were the days when skilled immigrants regarded Canada as the land of milk and honey. Those were the days when our dollar was more sought after than that of our mighty neighbour to the south. In five long years of Tory government the people have seen our prestige dwindle until our voice is no longer listened to, and our shores are no longer the goal of immigrants from prosperous Europe. Our money is no longer eagerly snapped up.
Canadians have sat back in amazement and watched the once proud Tory party accept, with gratitude, the assistance of the Social Credit party to stay in power. They accept the help of a splinter party whose very doctrine is fundamentally opposed to anything the Conservatives hold sacred. One would have thought that at least the Conservatives would have refrained from showing their glee.
As I listened first to the mover of the address in reply as he traced the industrial development of his constituency, and next to the seconder as he spoke with obvious pride of the industrial achievements of his country, I realized that I could not eulogize Verdun in either of these fields. The truth of the matter is that, situated as it is on the island of Montreal, the city of Verdun has long passed the time when it could lay claim to any achievement in the field of agriculture. Nor can we claim any fame in the field of industrialization, since the citizens of Verdun have long been happy to earn their living in the vast industries outside our boundaries. (Translation):
The Verdun riding is remarkable for the quality of its citizens. It has a population of
86,000	and is the third largest city in the province. But as regards bilingualism, Verdun is probably first in the country. For years, English Canadians and French Canadians have lived side by side in perfect harmony and nobody will make them believe that in the sight of the Divine Providence, there is any difference between the nations that live on this earth.
(Text):
Our degree of bilingualism can be traced directly to our vast recreational program. From an early age our French speaking and English speaking children play together on our many playgrounds, and when they reach the age of reason it is very difficult for any adult, already poisoned by the seeds of racial intolerance, to convince them that their French speaking or English speaking neighbour is not a wonderful person.
The Address-Mr. Mackasey (Translation):
As an English Canadian born in the province of Quebec, I have been for many years aware of the tremendous part played by the French Canadians in the building up of our country. Their faithfulness to Canada in the truly critical moments fills many pages of our history.
I am proud, Mr. Speaker, of being a citizen of Verdun and a resident of the province of Quebec. I boast of speaking, although with some difficulty, the tongue of my French Canadian friends.
(Text) :
There are two other accomplishments of the community of Verdun about which I wish to speak very briefly. I am proud of the fact, for instance, that the name of Verdun is known throughout the free world, and indeed behind the iron curtain. Within the boundaries of Verdun lies the famous Verdun Protestant hospital, the leading institution dedicated to the alleviation of mental illness. There a dedicated staff, under the direction of Dr. Roberts, has introduced new techniques and new methods of curing mental illness, methods based on kindness, compassion and the restoration of human dignity. These methods have been copied by other institutions throughout the world for there are no barriers, nor should there be any, to the exchange of ideas in this field.
The last item to which I wish to refer is the tremendous contribution Verdun made in the last war. It is on record that Verdun had the highest rate of enlistment per capita of any large city in Canada. Is it little wonder then, Mr. Speaker, that the citizens of Verdun resent certain political leaders expressing their admiration for the two greatest exponents of man's inhumanity to man?
Listening, as I did, quite attentively to the speech of the Prime Minister I found little of consequence. I think it is a little surprising when one realizes that this government had an abnormally long time at its disposal to prepare its program. While the opposition and the people of Canada cooled their heels waiting for the convening of parliament, the Prime Minister prepared a program that got progressively worse as the available time became shorter.
I did, however, hear him express the desire to balance the budget. This after five years of record deficits-not calculated deficits to relieve unemployment, but record deficits at a time when the unemployment rate was at an all time high in the history of Canada. I could not help thinking, again on a regional note, as I listened to the Prime Minister, that a week or two before the election our Prime Minister promised to visit the city of Verdun,

The Address-Mr. Mackasey as the Leader of the Opposition graciously did. We prepared the gold book, and all the traditional ceremonies that go with it, for our Prime Minister. What did he do? Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and his entourage sped through the city of Verdun by the shortest possible route and at the highest speed they could possibly go. Thousands of disappointed citizens were then left with the impression that the Tories had written Verdun off as being a bastion of Conservatism. On this latter conclusion I commend the Prime Minister for his foresight.
I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because the city of Verdun has as its proud city manager Mr. French, who has been able to balance the budget of our community for 24 consecutive years. Unfortunately for our Prime Minister, Mr. French is an avowed Liberal. So when the following evening came and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) rose to his feet, I listened very attentively. I have had occasion to hear his marvellous oratory on previous occasions. Here was the voice of French Canada in the Conservative government. Perhaps in his own inimitable style he could fill in the many voids in the Prime Minister's speech. After all, the Prime Minister had things on his mind when he delivered his speech. He knew from the evidence confronting him, documented evidence, concisely and accurately placed before the people by the Leader of the Opposition, that Canadians were aware the government had callously hidden the true facts about the economy of Canada before the election.
What did the Associate Minister of National Defence do instead? He used the valuable time at his disposal to attack the Liberal government of the province of Quebec, the very premier who, by his co-operation, by his sincere desire to help his people, had gladly co-operated on the removal of tolls on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges, probably the sole reason the Associate Minister of National Defence sits in parliament right now. I listened to the attack on the province of Quebec first started by the deputy leader of the Social Credit party and continued by the Associate Minister of National Defence and the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais).
The Lesage government, in the two years it has been in office, has done more to close the economic gap between Quebec and Canada than any other government in the history of that province. His reforms in the field of education, his introduction of the hospital plan, his exposure of the most corrupt political machine in the history of that province will result in an overwhelming Liberal victory
[Mr. Mackasey.)
in November. May we suggest that the Associate Minister of National Defence, instead of repaying favours to the remnants of this broken Union Nationale machine, should instead thank Mr. Lesage for keeping him in parliament.
I can document what I am saying, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to refer to La Presse of Thursday, May 10 with regard to the Champlain, Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. For hon. members outside the island of Montreal and the province of Quebec I would just like to take a moment or two to explain a little of the background. The Champlain bridge was conceived and started by the Liberal government in 1956-57. It was designed to alleviate the deplorable traffic conditions that existed on the two bridges, the Victoria and the Jacques Cartier. This magnificent structure was developed barely a mile or two from the two existing structures. The Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges at that time were being taxed beyond their capacity-and when we come to think of it, so are the Canadian people today.
Therefore it was agreed to construct the Champlain bridge in order to alleviate traffic on these existing arteries. I compliment the government for having agreed that it was necessary to relieve the traffic across the mighty St. Lawrence.
However, Mr. Speaker, is this new bridge fulfilling its role? Is the Champlain bridge carrying thousands of automobiles in and out of the island of Montreal daily? In fact, while automobiles still line up on the old bridges bumper to bumper, the new bridge is relatively unused. The trouble comes from two sources. First of all, in their haste to assure the Associate Minister of National Defence re-election, the government removed the tolls from the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges. This was a good move; it helped the people. But the government omitted to remove the tolls on the new bridge, which is situated just a few miles away. Consequently, those motorists situated equidistantly from the toll-free bridges and the new Champlain bridge still use the old arteries, for in this day and age of austerity 50 cents a round trip is still a lot of money.
This is what La Presse of Thursday, May 10 had to say with regard to the alleviation of tolls on two bridges and leaving them on the third:
The lack of logic is obvious. It was decided to build the Champlain bridge besides the two others to alleviate the traffic on these two latter bridges. Everyone understood the necessity. But what motorists who, having a choice between three bridges situated very close to each other, will seek out the only one on which they must pay? There will be some, of course, but they will be in the minority. Therefore these two bridges will

continue to be taxed to their full capacity. The purpose for which the new bridge was designed will not be achieved.
The following paragraph strikes me very forcefully, Mr. Speaker.
On the other hand, as the eventual minority of motorists using the new bridge will come from Verdun and St. Lambert-Laprairie, the toll will be for them a sort of indirect tax that will apply to them exclusively.
One of my confreres has suggested wryly that we surmise that this toll on the Champlain bridge will not last beyond the next election. Evidently the government does not intend to cede everything at once, in order to have some ammunition on hand for the next election. But in the present case one would suppose that reason would prevail. The Lesage government in particular has acted very impartially. It has not refused its collaboration on the excuse that it would help a rival government at the time of election.
I would suggest to the government that if it is their intention to remove the toll on the Champlain bridge just before the next election, they should do it in the next few days that remain at their disposal.
There is another problem in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, which I think exists right across this vast dominion of ours. It is the plight of a vastly growing segment of our population. I am referring to those young men-and I stress "young men"-who have reached the age of 40 and are out of work. Whilst the government is now discovering the need for vocational training and is attempting to turn out skilled labour for our industries, other very skilled workers, men who have worked for 20 years or so in the railways, in the aircraft industry and in the electronics field are being laid off because of automation or for other reasons. These men start out confident in their ability to find work. Has not the press blared out the need for skilled workers? But their confidence is soon destroyed as company after company refuses to hire them.
This was not because of any lack of talent but because these men are considered to be too old to work and too young for their old age pensions. Who says so? The architects of our company pension plan say so-these dealers in cold mathematics whose plans cannot tolerate the addition of new employees over the age of 40. Is this situation logical?
I did note in the speech from the throne some indication that the government has finally recognized this injustice. I would suggest that they discard for once the lines of political expediency and use the plan outlined in the Liberal program and elaborated upon by the Leader of the Opposition in a speech in the House of Commons last year. On this particular point, the government did finally recognize the difficulty, and I suggest they should use the few days at their disposal to implement without further delay a pension
The Address-Mr. Mackasey scheme which will end forever this insidious discrimination against our citizens in their best years of life.
When the Leader of the Opposition in his brilliant address suggested an extension of the federal share of expenditures in connection with slum clearance and urban renewal, members on the government benches ridiculed the proposal or referred him to the winter works program. But, in fact, Mr. Speaker, my community urgently needs some type of housing development for the use of its senior citizens, as do thousands of communities across Canada. It is of no use for the Tories to point to existing legislation in this regard. Private contractors, with few exceptions, are not using the legislation which is presently on the statute books pertaining to the construction of homes for the aged. The government itself, if necessary, should enter upon the construction of such homes. Every year, thousands of married couples in the twilight of their lives are forced to separate as the husband goes pathetically to an old men's home and the wife elsewhere. What we need, and need soon, is provision for our senior citizens to live out their lives together in security, comfort and privacy, and this might best be brought about through housing of a motel type such as is common in the Scandinavian countries. Our obligation to our senior citizens goes much further than simply raising old age pensions every few years. Private industry is not interested in the problem to any great degree, for if it is to build and operate these homes under present legislation it must charge rents far beyond the normal reach of our senior citizens.
I should like to point out briefly the experience of Toledo in the United States whose one-storey group of row housing units for older people represents one of the first of the new and imaginative approaches in this field in that country. Early in 1956, extensive research was begun to determine the extent for the need for public housing. I am sure the five points which I am about to mention and which represented the result, in part, of the survey, are deeply applicable at this time to Canada. These are:
1.	Existing public housing did not provide the type of living arrangements often needed by elderly families.
2.	Retirement acceleration had become an established practice in industry and many unprepared employees were being forced to retire.
3.	The number of recipients of social security benefits was mounting monthly.
4.	There were no opportunities for elderly families to continue living independently at a cost they could afford.

The Address-Mr. Mackasey
5.	Neither private nor public funds were available to meet the need and to make this type of development a reality.
Unfortunately, time does not permit me to go into the Toledo plan in further detail, but the subject is one which I am sure hon. members would agree must be of great concern to us all.
Mr. Speaker, when I walk along the miles of boardwalk for which Verdun is famous I can look across the water and see ships from all nations as they travel up the mighty St. Lawrence seaway, contemplated and executed by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) during the time when the present opposition was in power. When I listen to our good friends at the opposite end of this house saying that there is no difference between the two old parties I want to tell them this, that there is a basic difference. The Liberal party is a party of action and the Conservatives are a party of words. The record is here. Take, for example, unemployment insurance, a measure which members of the Social Credit party admire and want to stretch a little-in fact, I think most of them are sitting on their unemployment insurance now. Well, this was implemented by the Liberals in 1940. The veterans charter was brought in in 1953; family allowances in 1945; a national health program in 1948; old age pensions in 1951; old age assistance in 1951; allowances for the blind in 1951; and extension of the health grants in 1953; a measure to assist disabled persons in 1954; the second phase of the national health program in 1956; unemployment assistance in 1956; the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act in 1957, and
increased payments to children under the Family Allowances Act in 1957.
Lack of time does not permit me to give a complete list of all the accomplishments of the Liberals while in office. In closing, may I thank hon. members on both sides for the attention they have shown me in my maiden speech.

I congratulate you and offer you my best wishes.
I also wish to join all the other members of this house in congratulating the mover (Mr. Chaplin) and the seconder (Mr. Vincent) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, who gave such a good account of themselves.
